practice_questions.text:
Which rock type is most commonly found in UK upland areas?
A) Chalk
B) Granite
C) Clay
D) Sandstone
practice_questions.marks: B) Granite [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term sedimentary rock and give one UK example.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Accurate definition (rock formed from compressed layers of sediment) plus a correct UK example (chalk, limestone, sandstone, clay). Secure: Either accurate definition OR correct example with partial definition. Developing: Vague reference to layers without process. Emerging: Names a rock with no definition. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how past tectonic processes have helped to create UK upland landscapes.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Clear chain — ancient mountain-building (Caledonian/Variscan) created hard igneous and metamorphic rocks, which resist erosion, leaving uplands today. Secure: Two linked points (mountain-building produced hard rock; hard rock resists erosion). Developing: One process named without consequence. Emerging: Tectonics mentioned without link to landscape. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the distribution of UK uplands and lowlands.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Clear pattern (uplands NW, lowlands SE), one named upland and one named lowland, plus a comment on the dividing line (Tees-Exe). Secure: General pattern with two named places. Developing: Vague pattern with one place. Emerging: Names a place without a pattern. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why landscapes in different parts of the UK look so different from each other.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Three developed reasons spanning geology (rock type and resistance), past processes (glaciation, mountain building) and ongoing physical/human processes, with named UK examples. Secure: Two developed reasons with examples. Developing: Listed reasons without development. Emerging: One basic reason. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Assess the relative importance of physical and human processes in shaping a named UK landscape today.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument weighing physical (glaciation, weathering, river/slope action) against human (farming, forestry, settlement) processes for a clearly named landscape, with developed reasoning and a justified judgement. Secure: Both sides covered with examples but limited weighing. Developing: Mostly description of one side. Emerging: List-like; no judgement. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text: Roughly what percentage of the world’s population now lives in urban areas?
practice_questions.marks: A. 25% | B. 40% | C. 56% (correct) | D. 80% — 1 mark for C.

practice_questions.text: Define the term ‘urbanisation’.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: The increase in the proportion of a country’s population that lives in towns and cities. Secure: People moving into cities. Developing: Cities growing. Emerging: Vague reference.

practice_questions.text: Explain two pull factors that draw people to cities.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two from city jobs in industry and services, higher wages, hospitals/universities, electricity and clean water, perceived opportunity — with linked reasoning. Secure: Two factors with brief detail. Developing: Two factors named only. Emerging: One factor.

practice_questions.text: Describe the contrasting urbanisation rates of developed and emerging countries.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Developed countries (e.g. UK 84%) urbanised early during the Industrial Revolution and have plateaued; emerging countries are urbanising rapidly now (e.g. China 26% in 1990 to 64% in 2024). Secure: Two contrasts with figures. Developing: One contrast with figures. Emerging: Vague reference.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the UK’s major cities are clustered in particular regions.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Three developed reasons (coal in the Midlands and South Wales, iron in Sheffield, ports for global trade like Liverpool and Glasgow, fast water for Pennine mills, London’s position on the tidal Thames) with named cities. Secure: Two reasons with examples. Developing: Lists factors. Emerging: One factor only.

practice_questions.text: ‘Urbanisation has more disadvantages than advantages.’ To what extent do you agree? Use named examples.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two-sided answer with examples (informal settlements like Dharavi or favelas vs Shanghai economic growth from 7m to 26m), figures, recognising that outcomes depend on governance, with a justified conclusion. Secure: Both sides with examples but partial judgement. Developing: One-sided argument. Emerging: Generic statements.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is a quantitative method of recording channel change in a river investigation?
A) Annotated field sketch
B) Photograph of meanders
C) Tape measure of channel width
D) Verbal description by a resident
practice_questions.marks: C) Tape measure of channel width [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two pieces of secondary data that could be used in a coastal landscape investigation.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark each (max 2). Examples:
• A British Geological Survey geology map showing rock type along the coast
• A Shoreline Management Plan describing planned coastal management
• An aerial photograph showing cliff retreat over time
• Tide tables
• Wave-rider buoy data on wave height and direction
[Max 2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason for using systematic sampling in a river fieldwork investigation.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 3 marks for a developed reason.
Example: Systematic sampling means measurements are taken at fixed intervals along the river (1) which makes it easy to plan and ensures sites are evenly spread from upper to lower course (1), so changes in width, depth and velocity downstream can be compared fairly (1).
Alternative: speed of data collection in limited fieldwork time. [Max 3 marks]

practice_questions.text: A student timed an orange floating along 10 m of beach water in 22 seconds. Calculate the longshore drift velocity in metres per second, giving your answer to one decimal place. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks: 1 for correct formula, 2 for working, 1 for answer with units.
Formula: velocity = distance ÷ time = 10 ÷ 22 (1)
Working: 10 ÷ 22 = 0.4545... (1) (1 for correct calculation)
Answer: 0.5 m/s to 1 decimal place (1) [-1 if no units]
[Max 4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how a student could plan a coastal fieldwork investigation to test whether sediment becomes rounder along a beach. Refer to methods, sampling and risks.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 6 marks: 1–2 = simple list; 3–4 = some development; 5–6 = developed methods linked to question with sampling and risk addressed.
Indicative content:
• Stratified sampling along beach (e.g. 5 sites at 100 m spacing) so data represents whole stretch (1+1)
• At each site, randomly pick 10 pebbles, measure roundness using Powers' roundness chart and size with callipers (1+1)
• Annotated photographs at each site as qualitative evidence of pebble shape (1)
• Risk assessment: tide times checked, gloves worn, never sample alone (1)
• Compare mean roundness scores between sites to test whether pebbles round in the direction of longshore drift (1)
[Max 6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Evaluate the strengths and weaknesses of the methods you used in your physical fieldwork investigation. In your answer you should:
• name your investigation and its question
• describe two methods you used
• explain strengths and weaknesses of each
• reach a justified conclusion about the reliability of your data.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8): Sustained, well-evidenced evaluation. Names a specific investigation and question, describes two methods accurately, develops both strengths and weaknesses for each, reaches a justified judgement about reliability.
Secure (5–6): Clear evaluation. Names investigation, describes two methods; some strengths and weaknesses; conclusion present but partially justified.
Developing (3–4): Some evaluation. Investigation named, methods described in general terms; mostly one-sided; no clear conclusion.
Emerging (1–2): Simple description of methods. Limited evaluation. No investigation named.
Indicative content (river example): Strengths of width/depth measurement = simple, repeatable, gives clear data. Weaknesses = one day's snapshot, weather may not be typical, equipment error. Strength of sketches = qualitative context. Weaknesses = subjective. Conclusion should weigh whether two methods together gave a reliable answer.

practice_questions.text:
Which method is best described as quantitative human fieldwork?
A) Open-ended interview with the village postmaster
B) Pedestrian count of footfall at four points
C) Annotated photograph of a high street
D) Sketch of a vacant shop window
practice_questions.marks: B) Pedestrian count of footfall at four points [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two reasons why questionnaires are useful in rural fieldwork.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark each (max 2). Examples:
• They collect the views of residents that numbers alone miss.
• They allow comparison across age groups and length of residence.
• Closed questions give quantitative data; open questions give qualitative context.
• They can be repeated and standardised across investigators.
[Max 2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one way an environmental quality survey can be made more reliable.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 3 marks for a developed point.
Example: Calibrating scores before fieldwork (1) by having the whole class score one site together and agree what a 3 looks like (1) reduces variation between observers, so the data from different teams is comparable (1).
Alternative: triple sampling at each site, photo logging, increasing sample size, repeating at different times of day. [Max 3 marks]

practice_questions.text: A student counted 96 pedestrians in 12 minutes at a village high street. Calculate the mean rate of pedestrians per minute and per hour. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks: 1 for correct working per minute, 1 for value, 1 for working per hour, 1 for value with units.
Working: 96 ÷ 12 = 8 (1) per minute (1)
Working: 8 × 60 = 480 (1) per hour (1) [-1 if no units]
Alternative correct route: 96 × 5 = 480 per hour (60/12 = 5).
[Max 4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how a student could plan a fieldwork investigation into change in a UK city centre. Refer to methods, sampling and a secondary data source.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 6 marks: 1–2 = simple list; 3–4 = some development; 5–6 = developed methods linked to question with sampling and secondary source.
Indicative content:
• Land-use survey along a transect from the railway station to the inner ring road, recording each property as retail, services or vacant (1+1)
• Environmental quality survey at five sites scored on litter, graffiti, noise (1)
• Stratified sampling so sites cover both prime retail core and edge of CBD (1)
• Compare with ONS Census 2011 vs 2021 to show population and ethnicity change (1)
• Use a historic Goad map to show how shop occupancy has changed (1)
[Max 6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Evaluate the reliability of the data you collected in your human fieldwork investigation. In your answer you should:
• name the investigation and its question
• describe two methods you used
• explain factors that may have reduced reliability
• reach a justified conclusion about how reliable the data was overall.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8): Sustained, well-evidenced evaluation. Names a specific investigation and question, describes two methods, develops at least two reliability factors (e.g. sample size, observer bias, time of day, weather), reaches a justified judgement.
Secure (5–6): Clear evaluation. Investigation named with two methods; some reliability factors; conclusion present but partially justified.
Developing (3–4): Some evaluation. Investigation named, methods described in general terms; mostly one-sided; no clear conclusion.
Emerging (1–2): Simple description of methods. Limited evaluation. No investigation named.
Indicative content (urban example): Strengths = repeatable land-use categories, ONS data covers whole city. Weaknesses = small EQS sample, only one weekday, observer bias on subjective scores. Conclusion should weigh whether reliability is good enough to justify the conclusions drawn.

practice_questions.text: Which erosion process involves the force of compressed air in rock cracks?
practice_questions.marks: A. Abrasion  |  B. Attrition  |  C. Hydraulic action (correct)  |  D. Solution — 1 mark for C.

practice_questions.text: Define longshore drift.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sediment moved along a coastline in a zigzag pattern, caused by waves hitting at an angle. Secure: Sediment movement along the coast caused by angled waves. Developing: Movement of sand along the beach. Emerging: Vague mention of waves.

practice_questions.text: Explain how an arch becomes a stack.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sea erodes the base of the arch (hydraulic action, abrasion); weathering weakens the roof; the unsupported roof collapses, leaving a freestanding stack. Secure: Two linked stages. Developing: Mentions collapse without process. Emerging: Names landforms only.

practice_questions.text: Describe the formation of a spit.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Names longshore drift, explains direction (prevailing wind), notes how a change in coastline direction allows sediment to extend into open water, and adds the hooked end and sheltered marsh behind. Secure: Three of the above stages clearly. Developing: Mentions longshore drift without sequence. Emerging: Description without process.

practice_questions.text: Explain why some coastlines have headlands and bays while others do not.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Three developed reasons covering geological structure (discordant vs concordant), differential erosion of hard and soft rock, plus a UK example such as the Dorset coast. Secure: Two reasons with example. Developing: Vague references to rock differences. Emerging: Naming landforms without explanation.

practice_questions.text: Assess the influence of geological structure and wave type on the formation of UK coastal landforms.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument weighing geology (concordant/discordant, joints, hard/soft rock) against wave type (constructive/destructive), with named UK landforms and a justified judgement about which mattered most for a chosen example. Secure: Both factors covered with examples. Developing: Description-led, partial linkage. Emerging: One factor only.

practice_questions.text: Roughly how many people live in the local authority of Birmingham?
practice_questions.marks: A. 0.5 million | B. 1.16 million (correct) | C. 4 million | D. 9.7 million — 1 mark for B.

practice_questions.text: Define the terms ‘site’ and ‘situation’.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Site is the actual physical land on which a settlement is built (relief, soil, drainage). Situation is the position of that settlement relative to other places (roads, rivers, neighbouring cities). Secure: Both terms correct. Developing: One term correct. Emerging: Vague reference.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Birmingham’s situation in central England helped it grow into a major industrial city.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Central position made Birmingham the meeting point of national road, canal and rail networks; nearby coalfields supplied power; equidistant from major markets such as London and Manchester let it trade in all directions. Secure: Two linked stages. Developing: One reason. Emerging: Vague reference.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of a UK city’s Central Business District.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two from highest land values, tallest buildings, dominant office and retail use, transport interchange, low residential population, mix of historic civic buildings and modern skyscrapers — with a Birmingham example. Secure: Two named features. Developing: Two named only. Emerging: One feature.

practice_questions.text: Explain how Birmingham’s urban structure changes from the CBD to the urban-rural fringe.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Three developed comparisons covering land use (commercial → residential → family housing → industrial/commercial), building age (mixed-recent → Victorian → mid-20th century → post-1980), density and function, with named places (Brindleyplace, Sparkbrook, Edgbaston, Solihull). Secure: Two zones with named places. Developing: Lists zones. Emerging: One zone only.

practice_questions.text: ‘Connectivity matters more than site for a modern UK city.’ To what extent do you agree? Use Birmingham as an example.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two-sided answer with examples (M6 motorway hub, New Street rail, HS2, airport vs sandstone plateau, lack of navigable river), recognising that historical site mattered more before modern transport but situation/connectivity now matters more, with a justified conclusion. Secure: Both sides with examples but partial judgement. Developing: One-sided argument. Emerging: Generic statements.

practice_questions.text:
Which urban change describes people and businesses moving out of cities to rural areas?
A) Urbanisation
B) Suburbanisation
C) Counter-urbanisation
D) Re-urbanisation
practice_questions.marks: C) Counter-urbanisation [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define deindustrialisation.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: A clear two-part definition — the decline of manufacturing industry in a region, with reference to factory closures and job losses. Secure: Decline of manufacturing with one example consequence. Developing: Vague reference to factories closing. Emerging: Names industry without explanation.

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of international migration into a named UK city.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Names a city (Birmingham), identifies a specific cause (Commonwealth labour demand from the 1950s, EU enlargement 2004, family networks in Sparkbrook), and develops the link with a chain of reasoning. Secure: Cause and city named with one developed point. Developing: Cause stated without development. Emerging: Generic answer with no city named.

practice_questions.text: Describe how retailing has changed in a UK city you have studied.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Names Birmingham; describes CBD decline (closures of Debenhams, House of Fraser), the rise of out-of-town centres (Merry Hill 1985, Touchwood 2001), and the impact of online shopping; uses precise dates or figures. Secure: Three changes with a named city. Developing: Two general changes. Emerging: One vague change.

practice_questions.text: Explain the causes and impacts of inequality within a named UK city.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Three developed causes (deindustrialisation, migration patterns, retail decentralisation) linked to specific impacts in named wards (Ladywood vs Sutton Coldfield) with quantitative evidence (life expectancy gap of 9 years, child poverty figures). Secure: Two causes, two impacts, one named ward. Developing: Generic causes and impacts. Emerging: Inequality stated without explanation.

practice_questions.text: Assess the success of strategies used to improve quality of life in a named UK city.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument weighing at least two strategies (e.g. Perry Barr housing, Clean Air Zone, education investment) against each other in Birmingham, with chains of reasoning, named places and a justified judgement on which has done most. Secure: Two strategies with reasoning and a partial judgement. Developing: Strategies described without evaluation. Emerging: One strategy named only.

practice_questions.text: Which is an example of soft engineering?
practice_questions.marks: A. Sea wall  |  B. Rip rap  |  C. Beach nourishment (correct)  |  D. Groynes — 1 mark for C.

practice_questions.text: Define managed retreat.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: A coastal management approach where defences are removed or breached so the sea can flood low-value land, often creating salt marsh. Secure: Allowing the sea to flood low-value land deliberately. Developing: Letting the coast flood. Emerging: Vague reference to flooding.

practice_questions.text: Explain why hard engineering at one location can increase erosion further along the coast.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Groynes/sea walls trap or reflect sediment, so longshore drift carries less sand to coastlines downdrift; without that natural buffer, those coasts are exposed and erosion accelerates. Secure: Two linked points. Developing: Mentions sediment without process. Emerging: One vague point.

practice_questions.text: Describe the location of one named UK coastline that is rapidly eroding.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Names Holderness, places it East Yorkshire between Flamborough Head and Spurn Head, gives a length (~61 km) and an erosion rate (1.5–2 m/yr). Secure: Three of the above. Developing: Names the coast with one detail. Emerging: General reference only.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Holderness coast erodes so quickly.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Three developed reasons (soft boulder clay; long North Sea fetch generating destructive waves; north-easterly storm waves driving longshore drift) with reference to specific places (Mappleton, Hornsea). Secure: Two reasons with example. Developing: One reason. Emerging: Lists factors without explanation.

practice_questions.text: Assess the advantages and disadvantages of using hard engineering to defend a UK coastline you have studied.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument weighing benefits (protection of property, jobs) against costs (downdrift erosion, expense, visual impact), grounded in a named UK case study with figures, and a justified conclusion. Secure: Both sides covered with examples. Developing: Description-led, partial analysis. Emerging: One side only.

practice_questions.text:
Which presentation method best displays the proportion of land use categories in a city centre?
A) Line graph
B) Pie chart
C) Scatter graph
D) Climograph
practice_questions.marks: B) Pie chart [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two essential features of a hand-drawn choropleth map.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark each (max 2). Examples:
• A title describing what the map shows
• A clear key linking each shade to a value range
• A scale bar
• A north arrow
• Source/date of data
[Max 2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why a scatter graph is suitable for showing the relationship between distance downstream and pebble size.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 3 marks for a developed point.
Example: A scatter graph plots two paired variables (1) so each point shows pebble size at a particular distance downstream (1) — this lets you see whether pebbles get smaller as you move down the river by checking the direction of the trend (1).
[Max 3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Pebble sizes (cm) at one site: 4, 6, 8, 9, 11, 13, 15. Calculate the median and the range. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks: 1 for ordering or method, 1 for median value with units, 1 for range method, 1 for range value with units.
Median: data already in order; 7 values; middle value is 4th = 9 cm (1 method, 1 value)
Range: 15 − 4 = 11 (1 method, 1 value with cm) [-1 if no units]
[Max 4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how you would describe a graph showing changing pedestrian counts over a day in a UK town centre.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 6 marks: 1–2 = simple statement; 3–4 = some figures or pattern; 5–6 = TEA structure with trend, two figures and an anomaly explained.
Indicative content:
• Identify overall trend (e.g. footfall rises from morning to lunchtime, then falls into the evening) (1)
• Quote at least two figures (e.g. peak of 78/min at 12:30, falling to 41/min at 4 p.m.) (1+1)
• Identify and explain at least one anomaly (e.g. a dip during light rain) (1+1)
• Link to a wider geographical reason (e.g. lunchtime peak suggests workers + shoppers overlapping) (1)
[Max 6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Evaluate whether your fieldwork conclusion was a fair answer to your enquiry question. In your answer you should:
• name your investigation and question
• state the conclusion you reached
• explain how data and presentation supported it
• explain limitations that reduce confidence
• reach a justified judgement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8): Sustained, well-evidenced evaluation. Names investigation and question, states conclusion, links data to it with figures, develops at least two limitations, reaches a justified judgement.
Secure (5–6): Clear evaluation. Names investigation, states conclusion, some figures, considers limitations briefly, conclusion reached but partially justified.
Developing (3–4): Some evaluation. Investigation named, conclusion stated; limitations limited; no clear judgement.
Emerging (1–2): Simple description of conclusion only. No specific limitations or judgement.
Indicative content (river example): Conclusion supported because discharge tripled along course, pebbles rounded; limitation = single day, anomaly at site 3 not fully explained, sample size small. Judgement should weigh whether the conclusion is justified given those limits.

practice_questions.text:
Which feature best describes the site of Mumbai?
A) An inland river crossing
B) A peninsula on a deep natural harbour
C) A high mountain plateau
D) A coastal delta plain
practice_questions.marks: B) A peninsula on a deep natural harbour [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two pull factors that have attracted migrants to Mumbai.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two clear pull factors with brief specificity (e.g. construction jobs in BKC, work in textile and pharmaceutical factories, domestic service, IT and finance employment, opportunities in the informal economy). Secure: Two relevant factors named. Developing: One factor only. Emerging: Vague mention of work.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the structure of Mumbai differs from that of a typical UK city.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies that Mumbai is shaped by a peninsula into elongated zones (CBD at Fort/Nariman Point in the south, Dharavi and inner-city north of the centre, suburbs stretching up to Borivali) rather than concentric rings, with a clear linked reason. Secure: Two contrasts with reasoning. Developing: One contrast. Emerging: Generic comparison without place detail.

practice_questions.text: Describe the inequalities in quality of life found within Mumbai.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Names contrasting locations (Antilia/Altamount Road versus Dharavi), gives quantitative contrast (e.g. ~41% in informal settlements; infant mortality ~3x higher in low-income wards), and at least two contrasting indicators (housing, health, sanitation). Secure: Two contrasts with one statistic. Developing: General contrast without numbers. Emerging: One detail only.

practice_questions.text: Explain the causes and impacts of one challenge created by rapid urbanisation in Mumbai.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Three developed points covering causes (e.g. migration, lack of formal housing, weak planning enforcement) and impacts (overcrowding in Dharavi, disease risk, pressure on water and sewers) of one named challenge such as informal settlements or air pollution, with statistics. Secure: Two causes and two impacts with named place. Developing: One cause and one impact. Emerging: Names challenge only.

practice_questions.text: Assess the relative success of top-down and bottom-up strategies in managing the challenges of Mumbai’s growth.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument weighing top-down strategies (Dharavi Redevelopment, Mumbai Metro, Trans-Harbour Link) against bottom-up strategies (SPARC, Slum Networking Project, savings federations), using chains of reasoning, statistics and a justified judgement on which has done more for quality of life. Secure: Both approaches with examples and partial judgement. Developing: One approach detailed, the other named. Emerging: Generic descriptions only.

practice_questions.text: Which landform forms when a meander is cut off by a flood breaking across its neck?
practice_questions.marks: A. Levee  |  B. Floodplain  |  C. Oxbow lake (correct)  |  D. Gorge — 1 mark for C.

practice_questions.text: Define the term discharge in a river.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: The volume of water flowing past a point in the river per unit of time, usually measured in cumecs (m³/s). Secure: The volume of water in the river per second. Developing: How much water flows. Emerging: The flow.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a waterfall retreats upstream over time.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Soft rock below is eroded by hydraulic action and abrasion; the hard cap is undercut and unsupported; the cap collapses, so the waterfall retreats upstream, leaving a gorge. Secure: Two linked stages. Developing: Mentions collapse without process. Emerging: Names a waterfall only.

practice_questions.text: Describe how channel velocity changes from upper to lower course.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Velocity actually increases downstream (despite gentler gradient) because the channel is wider and deeper, with less friction; cites the Bradshaw model; gives a typical UK river example. Secure: Direction of change with reason. Developing: States increase without reason. Emerging: Vague.

practice_questions.text: Explain how erosion and deposition together form a meander.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Three developed points: faster flow on outside (erosion, river cliff); slower flow on inside (deposition, point bar); migration of curve over time, eventually leading to neck cut-off. Secure: Two stages with detail. Developing: Mentions inside/outside but no process. Emerging: Lists features.

practice_questions.text: Assess the relative importance of erosion and deposition in shaping the landforms of a river you have studied.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument weighing erosion (waterfalls, gorges, river cliffs) against deposition (point bars, levees, floodplains, oxbows) for a clearly named UK river, with linked landforms and a justified judgement. Secure: Both processes covered with examples. Developing: Description-led, partial weighing. Emerging: One process only.

practice_questions.text:
Roughly what is the UK population projected to reach by 2032?
A) 60 million
B) 65 million
C) 73 million
D) 90 million
practice_questions.marks: C) 73 million [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two sustainable transport options being used in the UK.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark each (max 2). Examples:
• Electric vehicles supported by 2030 ban on new petrol and diesel cars
• Rail electrification (e.g. Great Western route)
• Active travel infrastructure such as cycle lanes and the National Cycle Network
• Bus franchising (e.g. Greater Manchester's Bee Network)
• Clean Air Zones (e.g. Bristol)
[Max 2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one way that population growth puts pressure on UK ecosystems.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 3 marks for a developed reason.
Example: New housing for a growing population takes greenfield land (1) which fragments hedgerows and wetlands (1), reducing habitat connectivity and contributing to the decline of species such as hedgehogs and farmland birds (1).
Alternative: more pollution / more demand for fresh water / more tourism on countryside. [Max 3 marks]

practice_questions.text: In 2024, 20% of 1.95 million new UK car sales were battery electric. Calculate the number of electric cars sold. Show your working and give your answer to the nearest thousand.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks: 1 for method (× 0.2), 1 for working, 1 for answer, 1 for rounding correctly.
Working: 1,950,000 × 0.20 (1) = 390,000 (1+1)
Answer: 390,000 (already rounded to nearest thousand) (1)
Accept 390,000 EVs.
[Max 4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how tourism puts pressure on a UK National Park you have studied.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 6 marks: 1–2 = simple list; 3–4 = some development; 5–6 = developed chains with figures and named pressures.
Indicative content (Lake District):
• 18 million visitors a year (1) erode footpaths on Helvellyn requiring £1.5 million of National Trust repair (1+1)
• Second-home ownership pushes house prices to 11.6× local earnings (1) so young residents leave (1)
• Boats churn lake sediment and increase nutrient pollution (1)
• Park Authority responses include path repair and second-home limits (1)
[Max 6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Evaluate how successful UK sustainable transport policies are likely to be in cutting carbon emissions. In your answer you should:
• describe two UK sustainable transport options
• explain advantages of each
• explain drawbacks or limitations
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8): Sustained, well-evidenced evaluation. Names two UK examples (EV ban, Bee Network etc.), develops at least two advantages and two drawbacks, reaches a justified judgement using figures.
Secure (5–6): Clear evaluation. Two named options, advantages and drawbacks; conclusion present but partially justified.
Developing (3–4): Some evaluation. Options named in general terms, mostly one-sided; no clear judgement.
Emerging (1–2): Simple description of one option. No evaluation.
Indicative content: EVs cut tailpipe emissions but mining for batteries causes harm elsewhere; rail electrification faces high cost (HS2 scaled back 2023); franchising helps cities but rural areas left with declining bus services. Conclusion should weigh urban progress against rural lag and global vs local emissions.

practice_questions.text:
Which measure combines income, life expectancy and years of schooling into a single 0-to-1 score?
A) GDP per capita
B) Gini coefficient
C) Human Development Index
D) Corruption Perceptions Index
practice_questions.marks: C) Human Development Index [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define GDP per capita.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: The total value of goods and services produced by a country in a year, divided by its population, often adjusted for purchasing power parity. Secure: Total economic output divided by population. Developing: A measure of a country’s wealth. Emerging: Mentions money without precision.

practice_questions.text: Explain one limitation of GDP per capita as a measure of development.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies a clear limitation (ignores inequality / unpaid work / environmental damage / informal economy) and develops the consequence (e.g. a country with high GDP can still have poor average quality of life). Secure: Limitation named with linked impact. Developing: Limitation stated without development. Emerging: Vague comment on accuracy.

practice_questions.text: Describe the global pattern shown by HDI in 2024.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Names a top and a near-bottom performer (Switzerland 0.967, Niger 0.394), notes the broad north-south split with North America, Western Europe and East Asia at the top, sub-Saharan Africa at the bottom, and identifies anomalies (oil-rich Gulf states). Secure: Three quantitative points with named regions. Developing: Two general points. Emerging: One vague trend.

practice_questions.text: Explain how political and economic measures of development can give different results.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Three developed points using examples — e.g. Saudi Arabia (high GDP, lower CPI), Costa Rica (lower GDP, similar CPI to UK), India (rising GDP, low CPI). Explains why oil wealth, corruption or political freedom can pull rankings apart. Secure: Two developed points with examples. Developing: Difference noted but examples thin. Emerging: General contrast only.

practice_questions.text: ‘A single indicator can never measure development accurately.’ Assess this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument for and against, considering GDP, HDI, Gini, CPI and food/water security with statistics (UK HDI 0.940, Norway GDP per capita $130,000, etc.). Reaches a justified conclusion that triangulating measures is more reliable but a single composite (HDI) gets close. Secure: Both sides with examples and partial judgement. Developing: One-sided answer. Emerging: List of indicators without argument.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes a brownfield site?
A) Open farmland on the edge of a city
B) Land previously built on and now being redeveloped
C) National Park land protected by law
D) Land used for new motorways and railways
practice_questions.marks: B) Land previously built on and now being redeveloped [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two UK government strategies that aim to reduce the gap between regions.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark each (max 2). Examples:
• Northern Powerhouse (2014) linking northern cities through transport and devolution
• Levelling Up Fund (£4.8 billion since 2021)
• HS2 (originally to link London with northern cities, scaled back in 2023)
• Freeports at Teesside, Liverpool, Plymouth
• Devolved metro mayors in Manchester, West Midlands etc.
[Max 2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one advantage of building new housing on a brownfield site.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 3 marks for a developed advantage.
Example: Brownfield sites are usually within existing towns and cities (1) so new housing can use existing infrastructure such as roads, sewers and shops (1), reducing the need to build new ones and protecting countryside on the edge of the city (1).
Alternative: closer to jobs / less car dependency / regenerates derelict land. [Max 3 marks]

practice_questions.text: London produces 22% of UK output despite having 13% of the UK population. Calculate by how many percentage points London's share of output exceeds its share of population.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks: 1 for method, 1 for working, 1 for value, 1 for correct unit (percentage points).
Method: subtract population share from output share (1)
Working: 22 − 13 = 9 (1+1)
Answer: 9 percentage points (1)
Note: 'percentage points' is the correct unit (not %).
[Max 4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how high net migration affects life in a UK city.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 6 marks: 1–2 = simple list; 3–4 = some development; 5–6 = developed positive and negative impacts with figures.
Indicative content:
• Fills skills gaps in NHS (~17% of workforce overseas) (1+1)
• Adds workers to care homes and agriculture (1)
• Increases pressure on housing supply, raising rents (1)
• Increases school place demand and GP wait times in some areas (1)
• Boosts cultural diversity and small businesses (1)
• Boston, Lincolnshire is named example of high migration percentage change (1)
[Max 6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Evaluate whether brownfield development is a better choice than greenfield development for meeting UK housing need. In your answer you should:
• describe each type of development with a UK example
• explain advantages and drawbacks of each
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8): Sustained, well-evidenced evaluation. Names brownfield (e.g. Salford Quays, Olympic Park) and greenfield (Cambridge fringe, Milton Keynes) examples, develops at least two advantages and drawbacks of each, reaches a justified judgement.
Secure (5–6): Clear evaluation. Two named options, advantages and drawbacks; judgement reached but partially justified.
Developing (3–4): Some evaluation. Options named in general terms, mostly one-sided; no clear judgement.
Emerging (1–2): Simple description of one option. No evaluation.
Indicative content: Brownfield protects countryside, uses existing infrastructure, but costs more and risks gentrification. Greenfield is cheaper and quicker but consumes irreplaceable land and increases car dependency. Conclusion may say brownfield should be the priority where viable, but greenfield is needed at scale for the UK's housing shortfall.

practice_questions.text: Which is an example of soft engineering for river management?
practice_questions.marks: A. Channelisation  |  B. Sea wall  |  C. Floodplain zoning (correct)  |  D. Dam — 1 mark for C.

practice_questions.text: State two human causes of river flooding.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two clearly stated causes (e.g. urbanisation increasing surface runoff; deforestation reducing interception). Secure: Two valid causes briefly stated. Developing: One cause. Emerging: Vague mention of human activity.

practice_questions.text: Explain how urbanisation increases the risk of river flooding.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Concrete and tarmac are impermeable; rainwater cannot infiltrate; drains carry it directly into rivers; lag time falls and peak discharge rises. Secure: Two linked points. Developing: Mentions concrete without consequence. Emerging: One vague point.

practice_questions.text: Describe the location and main features of one named UK river.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Names a river (e.g. Tees), states source and mouth, gives a length, names two named features along the course (waterfall, meander, estuary). Secure: Three of the above. Developing: Names a river only. Emerging: Vague.

practice_questions.text: Explain why some UK river catchments flood more often than others.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Three developed contrasts: rock type (impermeable clay vs porous chalk), slope (upland steep vs lowland flat), land use (urban vs forested), with named examples. Secure: Two contrasts with examples. Developing: Lists factors without contrast. Emerging: One reason only.

practice_questions.text: Assess the effectiveness of using hard and soft engineering together to manage flood risk on a named UK river.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument weighing hard schemes (dam, channelisation) and soft schemes (washlands, restoration) for a clearly named river, with figures, advantages and limitations, and a justified conclusion. Secure: Both approaches with examples. Developing: Description-led. Emerging: One approach only.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is best described as a bottom-up development strategy?
A) The Three Gorges Dam
B) Grameen Bank micro-loans
C) The World Bank Mumbai rail corridor
D) The UN Sustainable Development Goals
practice_questions.marks: B) Grameen Bank micro-loans [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define international aid.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: The transfer of money, goods, services or expertise from one country (or organisation) to another, usually from a richer to a poorer country, with examples of bilateral, multilateral and NGO aid implied. Secure: Transfer of resources from one country to another. Developing: Help given to poorer countries. Emerging: Vague reference to charity.

practice_questions.text: Explain one historic cause of uneven global development.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies a clear historic cause (colonialism / conflict / debt) and develops a chain of reasoning — e.g. colonial economies were designed for raw-material export, so newly independent countries had infrastructure unsuited for internal development, slowing progress. Secure: Cause and one developed link. Developing: Cause stated without development. Emerging: Generic reference to history.

practice_questions.text: Describe two consequences of uneven development for quality of life.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two clear consequences (e.g. life expectancy gap Japan 84 vs CAR 53; food insecurity affecting 735 million people; 1.1 billion in informal settlements) with statistics and named examples. Secure: Two consequences with one statistic. Developing: One consequence with detail. Emerging: General comments only.

practice_questions.text: Explain the strengths and weaknesses of top-down development strategies.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Three developed points covering at least one strength and one weakness, using a named project (Three Gorges Dam, Lesotho Highlands Water Project) with quantitative evidence (1.3 million people displaced) and a clear linked impact. Secure: Two developed points with one example. Developing: Strengths or weaknesses noted without development. Emerging: One general point.

practice_questions.text: Assess whether top-down or bottom-up development is more effective at reducing uneven development.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument weighing top-down (named example, scale, debt risk) against bottom-up (Grameen, Practical Action) with chains of reasoning and a justified conclusion that combining the two often works best. Secure: Both approaches with examples and partial judgement. Developing: One approach detailed, the other named. Emerging: Generic descriptions only.

practice_questions.text: Which landform is an armchair-shaped hollow on a mountain side?
practice_questions.marks: A. Drumlin  |  B. Corrie (correct)  |  C. Arête  |  D. Truncated spur — 1 mark for B.

practice_questions.text: Define plucking as a glacial erosion process.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Meltwater at the base of a glacier freezes around loose rocks; as the ice moves it tears the rocks out of the bedrock. Secure: Ice freezes around rocks and pulls them out. Developing: Ice picks up rocks. Emerging: Vague reference to glaciation.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a pyramidal peak is formed.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Three or more corries develop on different sides of a mountain; their back walls retreat into the mountain by plucking and abrasion; eventually they leave a sharp pyramid-shaped peak. Secure: Two linked stages. Developing: Names corries without process. Emerging: Names the landform only.

practice_questions.text: Describe the location and main features of one glaciated upland landscape in the UK.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Names the Lake District, places it NW England, gives area or named lake/peak, plus a glacial landform such as Striding Edge or Wast Water. Secure: Three of these. Developing: Names the landscape only. Emerging: Vague reference.

practice_questions.text: Explain how human activity has affected a glaciated upland landscape you have studied.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Three developed impacts (e.g. sheep farming preventing tree regrowth; reservoirs drowning valleys; tourism causing footpath erosion) with named places and figures. Secure: Two impacts with examples. Developing: Lists impacts. Emerging: One impact only.

practice_questions.text: Assess the advantages and disadvantages of developing UK glaciated uplands for tourism, water supply or renewable energy.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument weighing economic and environmental advantages against disadvantages for at least two named uses, with developed examples and a justified conclusion that links to a named landscape. Secure: Both sides covered with examples. Developing: Description-led, partial weighing. Emerging: One use only.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is an example of soft engineering for UK flood management?
A) Thames Barrier in London
B) Concrete sea wall along the Yorkshire coast
C) Tree planting and 'leaky dams' upstream of Pickering
D) Tidal lock gates at the Boston Barrier
practice_questions.marks: C) Tree planting and 'leaky dams' upstream of Pickering [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two impacts of climate change already observed in the UK.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark each (max 2). Examples:
• Annual mean temperature has risen by around 1.0 °C in recent decades
• July 2022 was the first UK day above 40 °C (40.3 °C at Coningsby)
• Sea level around the UK has risen by about 18 cm since 1900
• Cairngorms ski season has shortened by around 30 days
• Floods from intense rainfall have become more frequent
[Max 2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one advantage of soft engineering for UK flood management.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 3 marks for a developed advantage.
Example: Soft engineering, such as tree planting in upper catchments (1), slows the rate at which rainwater reaches the river (1), reducing peak discharge so towns downstream are less likely to flood (1).
Alternative: Cheaper than concrete; ecological co-benefits (carbon, biodiversity); creates leisure spaces. [Max 3 marks]

practice_questions.text: The Pickering 'Slowing the Flow' scheme cost £3.2 million and reduced peak flow by 17% in storm conditions. Calculate the cost of reducing each 1% of peak flow, to the nearest thousand pounds.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks: 1 for method, 1 for working, 1 for value, 1 for rounding/units.
Method: divide £3,200,000 by 17 (1)
Working: 3,200,000 ÷ 17 = 188,235.29 (1+1)
Answer: £188,000 to nearest thousand pounds (1)
[Max 4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how managing a UK National Park causes conflict between different stakeholders.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 6 marks: 1–2 = simple list; 3–4 = some development; 5–6 = developed conflicts with named stakeholders and figures.
Indicative content (Lake District):
• Tourists want access to honeypots like Helvellyn (1) but eroded paths cost £1.5 million to repair (1)
• Local residents face house prices 11.6× earnings due to second homes (1) so young people leave (1)
• Farmers want subsidies for grazing while conservation groups want rewilding and peat bog restoration (1+1)
• Park authority must balance the Sandford Principle: conservation prioritised when in genuine conflict (1)
[Max 6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Evaluate whether UK responses to climate change focus too much on mitigation and not enough on adaptation. In your answer you should:
• describe one mitigation strategy and one adaptation strategy
• explain advantages of each
• explain limitations of each
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8): Sustained, well-evidenced evaluation. Names mitigation (Net Zero, offshore wind, 2030 EV ban) and adaptation (Pickering, Medmerry, urban tree planting) examples, develops advantages and limitations of each, reaches a justified judgement.
Secure (5–6): Clear evaluation. Two named strategies, advantages and drawbacks; conclusion present but partially justified.
Developing (3–4): Some evaluation. Strategies named in general terms; mostly one-sided; no clear judgement.
Emerging (1–2): Simple description of one strategy. No evaluation.
Indicative content: Mitigation tackles the cause (cuts CO2) but takes decades to bite. Adaptation copes with impacts already happening but does nothing to slow further change. Conclusion may say both are essential and that UK currently spends more on mitigation policy, while adaptation budgets struggle to keep up with rising flood risk.

practice_questions.text:
Roughly what was India’s population in 2024?
A) 0.5 billion
B) 1.0 billion
C) 1.43 billion
D) 2.5 billion
practice_questions.marks: C) 1.43 billion [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name two sectors of the Indian economy that have grown rapidly since 1991.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two clear sectors named with brief specificity (e.g. tertiary services, quaternary IT and software, manufacturing such as automotive or pharmaceuticals). Secure: Two sectors named. Developing: One sector named. Emerging: General reference to industry.

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason for uneven development within India.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies a clear reason (port access for southern states / longer history of education in Kerala / weaker governance in Bihar / climate-related agricultural difference) with chain of reasoning — e.g. Kerala’s long investment in literacy enabled a service-sector workforce, raising HDI to 0.781. Secure: Reason and one developed link. Developing: Reason stated without development. Emerging: General comment.

practice_questions.text: Describe how India’s population structure has changed over the last 30 years.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Names quantitative changes — fertility from ~4.0 (1990) to ~2.0 (2023), life expectancy from 58 to 70, narrower base of population pyramid, growing middle class (~430 million). Secure: Three changes with one statistic. Developing: General trend without numbers. Emerging: One change only.

practice_questions.text: Explain how geopolitics has affected India’s development.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Three developed points covering territorial disputes (Kashmir, Ladakh, Galwan Valley 2020), defence spending (~2.5% of GDP), trade agreements (UAE 2022, Quad alliance), and impact on foreign investment, with named examples and a clear linked impact. Secure: Two developed points. Developing: One point with example. Emerging: General comment on neighbours.

practice_questions.text: ‘The benefits of India’s rapid development outweigh the costs.’ Assess this view.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument balancing positives (poverty reduction, life expectancy +12 years, renewables 73 GW, IT services hub) against negatives (top 10% earn 57% of income, Delhi air pollution, groundwater depletion, female labour participation 27%) with chains of reasoning, named places and a justified judgement. Secure: Both sides with examples and partial judgement. Developing: One-sided answer. Emerging: List of impacts only.

practice_questions.text: At which latitude does sinking dry air create the world's deserts?
practice_questions.marks: A. 0°  |  B. 30° (correct)  |  C. 60°  |  D. 90° — 1 mark for B.

practice_questions.text: Define the Hadley cell.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: An atmospheric circulation cell between 0° and 30° in which warm equatorial air rises, releases rainfall, and sinks again at the subtropics. Secure: A circulation cell from equator to subtropics. Developing: Vague reference to circulation. Emerging: Names the cell only.

practice_questions.text: Explain why tropical rainforests are concentrated near the equator.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Intense solar heating warms equatorial air; it rises, cools and releases heavy rainfall; constant high temperatures and rainfall support rainforest. Secure: Two linked points. Developing: Mentions rain or heat without process. Emerging: Generic statement.

practice_questions.text: Describe the influence of the Gulf Stream on the UK's climate.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Names the Gulf Stream as a warm North Atlantic current; states it raises winter temperatures by several °C; compares with similar latitude in Canada (cooler); links to ice-free ports. Secure: Three of these. Developing: Mentions warming only. Emerging: Vague.

practice_questions.text: Explain why rainfall in the UK is much higher in the west than in the east.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Three developed reasons: prevailing south-westerlies pick up moisture over the Atlantic; western uplands force air to rise (relief rainfall); rain shadow effect on eastern side; named places (Cumbria 3,000 mm vs East Anglia <600 mm). Secure: Two reasons with examples. Developing: One reason. Emerging: Lists place names.

practice_questions.text: Assess the relative importance of latitude and ocean currents in shaping the UK climate.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument weighing latitude (limits solar energy received) against ocean currents (Gulf Stream raises winter temperatures), with figures and a justified judgement. Secure: Both factors covered with examples. Developing: Description-led. Emerging: One factor only.

practice_questions.text: Which of these is a natural cause of climate change?
practice_questions.marks: A. Methane from cattle  |  B. Burning of coal  |  C. Volcanic eruption (correct)  |  D. Cement production — 1 mark for C.

practice_questions.text: Define the enhanced greenhouse effect.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: The strengthening of the natural greenhouse effect by extra greenhouse gases released through human activity. Secure: Human emissions making the greenhouse effect stronger. Developing: Carbon dioxide trapping heat. Emerging: Vague reference to global warming.

practice_questions.text: Explain how ice cores tell us about past atmospheric CO2.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Snow falls year on year and traps tiny bubbles of air; the bubbles are sealed in ice as compaction continues; scientists drill cores and analyse the trapped gas, reading CO2 back over 800,000 years. Secure: Two linked points. Developing: Mentions ice cores without process. Emerging: Names ice cores only.

practice_questions.text: Describe the trend in atmospheric carbon dioxide since 1850.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: States CO2 has risen from ~280 ppm in 1850 to over 420 ppm today; identifies acceleration after 1950; gives a rate or compares with pre-industrial level. Secure: Two of these data points. Developing: General upward trend. Emerging: Names CO2 only.

practice_questions.text: Explain why human activities have led to the enhanced greenhouse effect.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Three developed sources (industry/energy burning fossil fuels; agriculture producing methane; deforestation releasing stored carbon and reducing future absorption) with examples. Secure: Two sources. Developing: One source. Emerging: Lists gases.

practice_questions.text: Assess the impacts of climate change on people and the environment so far.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument covering crop yields, sea-level rise and glacier retreat with figures and named places, recognising uneven effects on developed vs developing countries, and a justified judgement. Secure: Two impacts with examples. Developing: Description-led. Emerging: One impact.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is a renewable, biotic resource?
A) Coal
B) Wind
C) Timber
D) Iron ore
practice_questions.marks: C) Timber [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define a non-renewable resource.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: A clear two-part definition — a resource that does not replace itself on a human timescale, with a relevant example such as coal, oil or natural gas. Secure: Finite resource with one example. Developing: A resource that runs out. Emerging: Vague reference to running out.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the UK’s upland geography affects its water supply.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies relief rainfall on western/northern uplands (Lake District, Highlands) and develops the chain — moist Atlantic air rises, cools and releases rain — producing the wet north-west and dry south-east, with figures (Borrowdale ~3,300 mm vs London ~600 mm). Secure: One stage of reasoning with one figure. Developing: Generic mention of rain. Emerging: Vague comment on weather.

practice_questions.text: Describe the global distribution of fossil-fuel resources.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Names regions for oil (Middle East, Russia, Gulf of Mexico), coal (China, US, India, Australia) and natural gas (Russia, Iran, US), with one specific country example for each, plus a brief explanation that they form in ancient sedimentary basins. Secure: Two regions with examples. Developing: One region named. Emerging: Generic statement.

practice_questions.text: Explain how patterns of consumption can differ from patterns of supply for natural resources.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Three developed points using statistics (UK 2,800 kg oil-equivalent vs Bangladesh 270 kg; UK meat 80 kg vs India 4 kg per person), plus the role of trade in moving virtual water and energy across borders, with named examples. Secure: Two developed contrasts with figures. Developing: Difference noted but unsupported. Emerging: General comment on rich vs poor.

practice_questions.text: Assess how the exploitation of natural resources changes places.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument with named examples (Amazon deforestation, North Sea oil, Sahel desertification, Dubai groundwater) covering biodiversity, soil, air, water and economic transformation. Reaches a justified judgement on whether exploitation can be made sustainable. Secure: Two examples with reasoning and partial judgement. Developing: One example detailed. Emerging: List of impacts only.

practice_questions.text: Which of these is required for a tropical cyclone to form?
practice_questions.marks: A. Sea temperatures above 26.5°C (correct) | B. Cold polar air | C. Strong vertical wind shear | D. Latitude above 60° — 1 mark for A.

practice_questions.text: State two physical characteristics of a tropical cyclone.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained wind speed above 119 km/h AND a calm central eye 30–65 km wide / spiral rain bands hundreds of km across / very low central pressure. Secure: Two valid features. Developing: One feature. Emerging: Vague reference.

practice_questions.text: Explain why tropical cyclones form between 5° and 30° latitude.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Ocean temperatures reach 26.5°C in this band giving the energy needed; Coriolis force is strong enough to spin the rising air column; the equator itself has too little Coriolis. Secure: Two linked stages. Developing: One condition only. Emerging: Vague reference.

practice_questions.text: Describe two contrasting impacts that Hurricane Katrina (2005) had on New Orleans.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two from social (1,800 deaths, displacement of poorer Black communities, Superdome conditions), economic ($125 billion damage, insurance crisis), or environmental (toxic floodwater, oil spills) with figures. Secure: Two impacts named with figures. Developing: Two impacts no figures. Emerging: One impact.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the impacts of tropical cyclones differ between developed and developing countries.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Three developed reasons (building codes, evacuation transport, warning systems, insurance, hospital capacity, international aid dependence) with case-study figures from Katrina and Idai. Secure: Two reasons with examples. Developing: Lists differences. Emerging: One difference only.

practice_questions.text: ‘Wealth, not wind speed, decides who dies in a tropical cyclone.’ To what extent do you agree? Use named examples to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two-sided answer comparing Katrina and Idai with specific evidence (death tolls, GDP loss, infrastructure quality), recognising wind speed/surge does still matter, and reaching a justified conclusion. Secure: Comparison with examples but partial judgement. Developing: One-sided argument. Emerging: Generic statements with no examples.

practice_questions.text:
Which of these is a non-renewable energy resource?
A) Solar
B) Wind
C) Uranium for nuclear power
D) Hydroelectric power
practice_questions.marks: C) Uranium for nuclear power [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two reasons why global energy demand has risen since 1924.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two clear reasons (population growth from ~2 billion to ~8 billion, rising wealth and home appliance use, technology such as cars, data centres and electric heating). Secure: Two reasons named. Developing: One reason. Emerging: Vague reference to growth.

practice_questions.text: Explain one advantage of natural gas as part of the UK’s energy mix.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies a clear advantage (lower CO₂ than coal, flexible to balance variable renewables, existing pipeline infrastructure) and develops the reasoning — e.g. gas plants ramp up in minutes when wind drops, helping keep the lights on without bringing back coal. Secure: Advantage and one developed link. Developing: Advantage stated without development. Emerging: General comment.

practice_questions.text: Describe the changes in the UK’s electricity mix between 1990 and 2023.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Names key shifts — coal from ~65% to under 2% (closure of Ratcliffe-on-Soar 2024), rise of natural gas, expansion of offshore wind to ~29%, decline in nuclear, rise of biomass at Drax — with at least three figures. Secure: Three changes with two figures. Developing: Two changes named. Emerging: One change only.

practice_questions.text: Explain the impacts of one renewable and one non-renewable energy resource.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Three developed impacts using named examples (e.g. Three Gorges Dam displaced 1.3 million people; Deepwater Horizon spilled 4.9 million barrels), covering social, economic and environmental dimensions, with a chain of reasoning. Secure: Two developed impacts. Developing: One impact each side. Emerging: Generic positives and negatives.

practice_questions.text: Assess whether top-down or bottom-up strategies are more effective in moving the UK towards sustainable energy.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument weighing top-down (Hinkley Point C, Hornsea 2, Contracts for Difference) against bottom-up (Boiler Upgrade Scheme, Smart Export Guarantee, community energy) with chains of reasoning, statistics and a justified judgement that both are needed. Secure: Both approaches with examples and partial judgement. Developing: One approach detailed. Emerging: Generic descriptions.

practice_questions.text: Which type of drought happens when rainfall stays well below the long-term average?
practice_questions.marks: A. Hydrological | B. Meteorological (correct) | C. Agricultural | D. Socio-economic — 1 mark for B.

practice_questions.text: Define the term ‘drought’.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: A long period of below-average rainfall that causes water shortages, damaging crops, ecosystems and livelihoods. Secure: Long period of below-normal rainfall causing water shortages. Developing: A dry period. Emerging: Vague reference.

practice_questions.text: Explain how El Niño can trigger drought in some parts of the world.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: El Niño flips Pacific sea-surface temperatures so warm water shifts east; this changes atmospheric circulation, causing dry sinking air over eastern Australia, Indonesia and southern Africa instead of normal rising rainfall. Secure: Two linked stages. Developing: Names El Niño only. Emerging: Vague reference.

practice_questions.text: Describe two human causes of drought.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two from over-extraction for agriculture (Aral Sea shrinking from cotton irrigation), unsustainable dam building (Mekong reduced flow), or deforestation reducing the moisture cycle (Amazon longer dry seasons) — with examples. Secure: Two named with brief detail. Developing: Two named only. Emerging: One cause.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the impacts of drought vary between developed and developing countries.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Three developed reasons (insurance access, government aid budgets, food import capacity, irrigation infrastructure, water rationing rather than starvation) with figures from Australia and Ethiopia. Secure: Two reasons with examples. Developing: Lists differences. Emerging: One difference only.

practice_questions.text: ‘Top-down responses are more effective than bottom-up responses to drought.’ To what extent do you agree? Use named examples.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two-sided argument with named top-down (desalination plants, dams, inter-basin transfers) and bottom-up (rainwater harvesting, drought-tolerant crops, sand dams) responses, recognising that wealthier countries can afford top-down while bottom-up suits low-income contexts, with a justified conclusion. Secure: Both sides with examples but partial judgement. Developing: One-sided argument. Emerging: Generic statements.

practice_questions.text:
Which country uses the highest proportion of its freshwater in agriculture?
A) United Kingdom
B) Germany
C) India
D) Singapore
practice_questions.marks: C) India [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term water deficit.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for a basic answer; 2 marks for a developed answer.
• 1 mark: when demand for water is greater than supply.
• 2 marks: when the demand for water in a place exceeds the available supply, often because rainfall is low, population is high, or both. [Max 2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why the UK has water supply problems.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 3 marks for a developed reason with explanation.
Example: The UK’s rainfall is unevenly distributed (1) — most rain falls in the north and west, but population is concentrated in the south-east (1) — so water has to be transferred long distances or supply runs short in dry summers (1).
Other accepted reasons: ageing infrastructure (around 20% leakage); seasonal mismatch between rainfall and demand; rising population in the south-east. [Max 3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Study a graph showing global water use by sector in 1975 and 2025. Describe the change in agricultural water use and one other change shown.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks: 2 for trend with data, 2 for a second observation/anomaly.
Example: Agricultural water use has roughly doubled in volume between 1975 and 2025 (1), although as a share of total use it has fallen from around 80% to around 70% (1). Industrial use has grown most rapidly in percentage terms, especially after 2000 (1), driven by industrialisation in emerging economies such as China and India (1).
[Quote at least one figure for full marks. No data = max 2.]

practice_questions.text: Explain how a growing population in an emerging country causes water supply problems.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 6 marks. 1–2 = simple points without development. 3–4 = developed points but limited chains of reasoning. 5–6 = developed chains linking population growth to specific impacts.
Example chain: Population growth increases demand for drinking water and sanitation (1), and for irrigated food (1), so groundwater is pumped faster than rainfall recharges aquifers (1). Falling water tables mean wells run dry (1) and rivers such as the Yamuna receive concentrated pollution (1) because there is less flow to dilute waste (1). The result is rising waterborne disease and conflict over remaining sources. [Max 6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Evaluate the success of one country's attempts to manage its water resources sustainably. In your answer you should:
• name the country and describe its strategies
• explain advantages of these strategies
• explain drawbacks or limitations
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8): Sustained, well-evidenced evaluation. Names a specific country (e.g. Singapore), describes at least two strategies in detail with statistics, develops both advantages and drawbacks, reaches a justified judgement. Spelling, punctuation, grammar accurate.
Secure (5–6): Clear evaluation. Country named with two strategies; some statistics; both sides considered but development uneven; conclusion reached but partially justified.
Developing (3–4): Some evaluation. Country named, strategies described in general terms; mostly one-sided; no clear conclusion.
Emerging (1–2): Simple description of one strategy. Limited evaluation. No country case or no judgement.
Indicative content (Singapore): Four National Taps strategy, NEWater meets ~40% of demand, sharply rising tariffs encourage conservation. Drawbacks: imports still needed, energy-intensive desalination, expensive. Conclusion should weigh self-sufficiency progress against costs.

practice_questions.text: Which factor most strongly controls the global distribution of biomes?
practice_questions.marks: A. Soil colour | B. Climate (correct) | C. Tectonic plate boundaries | D. Length of day — 1 mark for B.

practice_questions.text: Define the term ‘biosphere’.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: The total of all living things on Earth, considered as a system that supplies resources and regulates atmosphere, water and carbon cycles. Secure: All living things on Earth as a system. Developing: Living things on Earth. Emerging: Vague reference.

practice_questions.text: Explain why tropical rainforests are found near the equator.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: The Hadley cell makes warm moist air rise at the equator; this air cools and releases heavy rainfall year-round; combined with high temperatures, this supports the lush plant growth typical of tropical rainforest. Secure: Two linked stages. Developing: One condition only. Emerging: Vague reference.

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways in which the biosphere provides resources for people.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two from food (75% from 12 plant species), medicine (e.g. aspirin from willow, Taxol from Pacific yew), building materials (timber, bamboo) or fuel (firewood for 2.4 billion people, bioenergy 6% of UK electricity) — with brief detail. Secure: Two named with brief detail. Developing: Two named only. Emerging: One resource.

practice_questions.text: Explain how human activities are degrading UK marine ecosystems.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Three developed reasons (industrial trawling cutting North Sea cod stocks, sewage pollution closing beaches, oil and gas seabed damage, plastic accumulation, coastal development) with named places or figures. Secure: Two reasons with examples. Developing: Lists impacts. Emerging: One impact only.

practice_questions.text: ‘The UK’s ecosystems are more important for biodiversity than for resources.’ To what extent do you agree? Use named examples.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two-sided answer with examples (e.g. Flow Country carbon storage, chalk grassland biodiversity, £1bn fishing industry, timber production), recognising that resource and biodiversity values overlap, with a justified conclusion. Secure: Both sides with examples but partial judgement. Developing: One-sided argument. Emerging: Generic statements.

practice_questions.text: Which adaptation helps rainforest leaves shed heavy rainfall quickly?
practice_questions.marks: A. Buttress roots | B. Lianas | C. Drip tips (correct) | D. Camouflage — 1 mark for C.

practice_questions.text: State two abiotic features of the tropical rainforest ecosystem.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two from high temperature (around 27°C year-round), high rainfall (2,000–3,000 mm), thin nutrient-poor soils, year-round growing season, high humidity. Secure: Two valid features. Developing: One feature. Emerging: Vague reference.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the nutrient cycle differs between tropical rainforests and deciduous woodlands.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Rainforest biomass is huge but soil and litter stores are tiny because rapid decomposition recycles nutrients straight back into trees; deciduous woodlands have more balanced stores because slow winter decomposition builds a deep litter layer that releases nutrients each spring. Secure: Two linked stages. Developing: One difference. Emerging: Vague reference.

practice_questions.text: Describe two adaptations that help animals survive in a deciduous woodland.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two from migration (cuckoos, swallows leaving for warmer climates), hibernation (hedgehogs and dormice slowing metabolism through winter), food storage (squirrels caching nuts), camouflage to match seasonal colours — with explanation of why each works. Secure: Two named with brief detail. Developing: Two named only. Emerging: One adaptation.

practice_questions.text: Explain the economic and social causes of tropical rainforest deforestation.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Three developed causes (cattle ranching for beef, soya plantations for animal feed, hardwood logging, gold mining, smallholder farming along new roads, population pressure) with named regions. Secure: Two causes with examples. Developing: Lists causes. Emerging: One cause only.

practice_questions.text: ‘Sustainable management of forests can only succeed in wealthy countries.’ To what extent do you agree? Use one named tropical rainforest region and one UK example.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two-sided answer comparing Costa Rica and the New Forest with figures (forest cover increase, ecotourism revenue, visitor management), recognising that both wealthy and middle-income countries can succeed if governance is strong, with a justified conclusion. Secure: Both sides with examples but partial judgement. Developing: One-sided argument. Emerging: Generic statements.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is an example of a honeypot site in the Lake District?
A) Mardale Green
B) Ennerdale
C) Windermere
D) Honister
practice_questions.marks: A. Mardale Green  |  B. Ennerdale  |  C. Windermere (correct)  |  D. Honister — 1 mark for C.

practice_questions.text: State two land use conflicts found in glaciated uplands.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two distinct conflicts clearly stated (e.g. farming versus conservation over overgrazing; tourism versus residents over affordable housing). Secure: Two valid conflicts briefly stated. Developing: One conflict. Emerging: Vague mention of disagreement.

practice_questions.text: Explain why ribbon lakes in glaciated troughs are well-suited for use as reservoirs.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Glacial troughs are deep (glaciers eroded to depth); ribbon lakes are long and narrow with a natural rock bar or moraine at the end creating a natural dam; steep impermeable valley sides reduce seepage. Secure: Two linked points. Developing: States they are deep without explaining why. Emerging: One point only.

practice_questions.text: Describe the economic importance of tourism to the Lake District National Park.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Gives visitor number (~17-19 million/year), annual economic value (~£2.3 billion), number of jobs (~18,000), and a specific honeypot location. Secure: Three of these. Developing: States tourism is important with one figure. Emerging: Vague reference to visitors.

practice_questions.text: Explain how tourism has created both economic and environmental problems in a glaciated upland you have studied.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Three developed impacts covering both economic (housing unaffordability, seasonal employment) and environmental (footpath erosion on Helvellyn, traffic congestion on A591, water quality decline in Windermere) with named places and figures. Secure: Two impacts with examples. Developing: Lists impacts without development. Emerging: One impact only.

practice_questions.text: Assess how effectively the Lake District National Park is managed to balance tourism with conservation of its glaciated landscape.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument weighing at least two management strategies (e.g. Fix the Fells footpath repair, LDNPA planning controls, shuttle buses and visitor dispersal to Ennerdale/Duddon) with specific named examples, statistical evidence, advantages and limitations, and a justified conclusion about overall effectiveness. Secure: Two strategies with evidence, some weighing. Developing: Describes strategies without assessing effectiveness. Emerging: One strategy or generic answer.
